diagnoses.rule_anchor: Apply the same lesser-of rule to specific provisions; never report a ceiling when the asset is worth less.
For the whole asset, report the lesser of its value and $300 for one debtor, or the lesser of its value and $600 for jointly owned property when each spouse claims the exemption.
Do not apply subsection (b) to business-use or nondebtor property, omit it because a specific subsection applies, or report its ceiling above the asset's value.
Return one claim only for each exact operative category the facts establish, using the lesser of whole-asset value and its stated ceiling.

Do not blindly report $4,000 when the paragraph (d) amount is unused, report more than the vehicle's value, apply the motor-vehicle provision to nonvehicles, or infer a married-couple ceiling from this one-debtor rule.

before.when: Federal exemptions under 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) are allowable and the asset is debtor-owned property.
before.procedure:
For each asset, output one separate § 522(d)(5) alternative and retain every applicable specific federal alternative. The claim for the whole asset is always the lesser of its value and the applicable ceiling: § 522(d)(5) uses $15,425 for one debtor or $30,850 for jointly owned property of two joint debtors when both full ceilings are available. Apply the same lesser-of rule to specific provisions; never report a ceiling when the asset is worth less. Section 522(d)(3) is capped at $700 per item. For jointly owned jewelry of two joint debtors, § 522(d)(4) protects the lesser of the whole value and $3,750; its one-debtor ceiling is $1,875.
Execution example: For a hypothetical jointly owned vehicle worth $20,000, retain the vehicle citation at its own $4,450 ceiling and add § 522(d)(5) at $20,000. For a hypothetical low-value specific-category item, both its specific claim and wildcard claim must be limited to the item's value.
before.avoid_when: Do not use § 522(d)(5) when federal subsection (d) exemptions are unavailable or the asset is not debtor property. Do not omit it because another federal provision applies, substitute its amount for another provision, copy any ceiling above the asset's value, or duplicate a citation.

after.when: Federal exemptions under 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) are allowable and the asset is debtor-owned property.
after.procedure: Make independent passes for § 522(d)(5) and every matching specific provision. Add (d)(5) to every asset, including a residence, at the lesser of whole-asset value and $15,425 for one debtor or $30,850 for jointly owned property of two joint debtors. For specific claims, use the asset value or that provision's benchmark ceiling, whichever is less: do not double the $27,900 residence, $4,450 vehicle, or $700-per-item household-goods ceiling merely because there are two debtors; jewelry uses $1,875 for one debtor or $3,750 for jointly owned jewelry of two joint debtors. Paragraph (d)(3) requires an enumerated household category and does not cover firearms or jewelry.
after.avoid_when: Do not use (d)(5) when federal subsection (d) exemptions are unavailable or the asset is not debtor property. Do not omit it because a specific provision applies, treat a cap as defeating eligibility, classify a firearm or jewelry under (d)(3), report more than the whole asset value, or duplicate a citation.

before.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the asset is debtor-owned personal property used for personal rather than business purposes.
before.procedure:
Use two independent passes. First, add exactly one § 12-1001(b) entry to every such asset—including animals, clothing and property lacking a specific category—and report the lesser of whole-asset value and $4,000 for one debtor or $8,000 for jointly owned property of two debtors. Second, retain each matching specific subsection with its own amount: necessary wearing apparel under (a), a motor vehicle under (c), and a professionally prescribed health aid under uncapped (e).
Execution example: A hypothetical prescribed personal-use aid worth $3,000 receives both (b) at $3,000 and (e) at $3,000; hypothetical clothing likewise retains both (a) and (b).
before.avoid_when: Do not apply subsection (b) to business-use or nondebtor property, omit it because a specific subsection applies, or report its ceiling above the asset's value. Do not infer subsection (d) without stated trade use, and do not duplicate citations.

after.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the asset is debtor-owned personal property, including an item whose stated trade use also enables subsection (d).
after.procedure: Use independent passes. Add exactly one § 12-1001(b) alternative to each such asset, including vehicles, clothing, animals, uncategorized personal goods, and stated trade tools; use the lesser of whole-asset value and $4,000 for one debtor or $8,000 for jointly owned property of two debtors. Then retain matching specifics: uncapped necessary apparel under (a), a motor vehicle under (c) at no more than $2,400 for the whole asset, trade tools under (d) at no more than $1,500 for one debtor or $3,000 for two joint debtors, and prescribed health aids under uncapped (e).
after.avoid_when: Do not apply (b) to real or nondebtor property, omit it because (a), (c), or (d) also applies, substitute the (b) ceiling for a specific subsection, double the (c) ceiling for joint debtors, infer (d) without stated trade use, exceed the asset value, or duplicate a citation.

before.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and the asset is property of the judgment debtor.
before.procedure:
Make a separate § 8123 pass over every asset, including vehicles, household goods, jewelry, animals, clothing and business-use property. Add exactly one § 8123 entry without removing federal or specific Pennsylvania alternatives. For the whole asset, report the lesser of its value and $300 for one debtor, or the lesser of its value and $600 for jointly owned property when each spouse claims the exemption.
Execution example: A hypothetical jointly owned item worth $180 receives a § 8123 claim of $180, not $600; an item worth more than $600 receives $600.
before.avoid_when: Do not apply § 8123 outside the debtor's property or a Pennsylvania namespace. Do not replace it with the parent citation § 8124(a), copy its ceiling when the asset is worth less, or treat the absence of a specific Pennsylvania category as a reason to omit § 8123. Section 8124(a)(4) remains limited to a commissioned officer's or enlisted person's uniform and accoutrements.

after.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and the asset is property of the judgment debtor.
after.procedure: For every asset, add one independent § 8123 entry without removing federal or specific Pennsylvania alternatives. First choose the ceiling from the debtor count: $300 for one debtor, or $600 for jointly owned property when both spouses claim. Then report the lesser of that ceiling and the whole asset's value; repeat this calculation for each asset rather than copying the ceiling.
after.avoid_when: Do not apply § 8123 outside debtor property or Pennsylvania, use $600 for one debtor, report a ceiling above the asset's value, replace § 8123 with § 8124(a), or omit § 8123 because a specific category is absent or present. Section 8124(a)(4) remains limited to a commissioned officer's or enlisted person's uniform and accoutrements.

before.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and an asset is being evaluated under the supplied Arizona property provisions.
before.procedure: Return one claim only for each exact operative category the facts establish, using the lesser of whole-asset value and its stated ceiling. Section 33-1123 covers household furniture, furnishings, goods, electronics and appliances only when not otherwise specifically prescribed. Use § 33-1125(1) only for wearing apparel, (2) for musical instruments, (8) for one motor vehicle, (9) for a factually established prescribed prosthetic or medical aid, (10) for firearms, and (11) for domestic animals or household pets. Section 33-1125(4) is limited to engagement and wedding rings. Arizona's opt-out provision excludes federal § 522(d) alternatives.
before.avoid_when: Do not classify jewelry as apparel, extend the ring provision to other jewelry, treat a specifically listed instrument or apparel item as § 33-1123 property, cite coordination or heading provisions, add zero-value claims, duplicate claims, or include federal exemptions.

after.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and an asset is being evaluated under the supplied Arizona property provisions.
after.procedure: Return one claim for each exact operative category established by the facts, using the lesser of whole-asset value and the applicable ceiling. Section 33-1123 covers household furniture, furnishings, goods, electronics and appliances only when not otherwise specifically prescribed. Use § 33-1125(1) only for wearing apparel, (2) for musical instruments, (8) for one motor vehicle, (9) for a factually established prescribed prosthetic or medical aid, (10) for firearms, and (11) for domestic animals or household pets; (4) is limited to engagement and wedding rings. For married joint debtors, § 33-1121 permits their individual article exemptions to be combined in the same jointly owned asset, but return only the operative property citation. Arizona's opt-out excludes federal § 522(d) alternatives.
after.avoid_when: Do not treat a ceiling as an eligibility test, classify jewelry as apparel, extend the ring provision to other jewelry, put a specifically listed instrument or apparel item under § 33-1123, cite § 33-1121 or a heading provision as the asset exemption, add zero-value claims, duplicate claims, or include federal exemptions.

after.when: Wisconsin exemptions are allowable and the debtor-owned asset is an occupied homestead.
after.procedure: Include Wis. Stat. § 815.20(1). Report the lesser of the whole homestead value and $75,000 for one debtor; for a jointly owned homestead of two spouse debtors, combine their statutory exemptions and use a $150,000 whole-asset ceiling.
after.avoid_when: Do not leave a spouse's half-interest or $75,000 as the final amount for a qualifying jointly owned homestead, exceed the whole asset value, or apply the provision to property that is not an occupied homestead.

before.when: Wisconsin exemptions are allowable, the asset is a motor vehicle, and the case has one debtor.
before.procedure: Include Wis. Stat. § 815.18(3)(g). Its ceiling is $4,000 plus any unused amount of the $12,000 consumer-goods exemption in paragraph (d). Because EV evaluates each asset-exemption pair independently without allocating an aggregate across other assets, use a $16,000 ceiling when the facts do not establish another use of paragraph (d), then report the lesser of the vehicle's whole value and that ceiling.
before.avoid_when: Do not blindly report $4,000 when the paragraph (d) amount is unused, report more than the vehicle's value, apply the motor-vehicle provision to nonvehicles, or infer a married-couple ceiling from this one-debtor rule.

after.when: Wisconsin exemptions are allowable and the asset is a debtor-owned motor vehicle.
after.procedure: Include Wis. Stat. § 815.18(3)(g). Its ceiling is $4,000 plus unused § 815.18(3)(d) consumer-goods capacity. Because EV evaluates each asset-law pair independently, use $16,000 for one debtor when no other use is established. Under § 815.18(8), two spouses may combine those exemptions in the same jointly owned vehicle, producing a $32,000 whole-asset ceiling. Report the lesser of the vehicle's whole value and the applicable ceiling.
after.avoid_when: Do not stop at the base $4,000 when paragraph (d) capacity is unused, use the one-debtor ceiling for a jointly owned vehicle of two spouse debtors, exceed the vehicle's value, or apply the provision to a nonvehicle.
